1859: aluminium cost $37 a kilo, about the price of silver, though it is the most common metal in Earth's crust. Napoleon the Third served his best guests with it.

At Oberlin College, Professor Frank Jewett said whoever found a cheap way to make it would make a fortune. His student Charles Martin Hall, 22, went home to the family woodshed. Chemists pried aluminium out of its ore with sodium, slow and ruinous. Hall used electricity: dissolve the ore in molten salt, run a current, let the metal collect.

5 salts failed. Then cryolite, melted at 1,000 degrees Celsius, dissolved the ore. On 23 February 1886 he cracked open the crucible and found beads of aluminium. His process took the price to 66 cents a kilo, world output went from under 4 tonnes a year to 73.8 million, and every kilo of new aluminium is still made his way. Today it makes 420 billion drink cans a year.

Builders wanted. The Ad Astra Fellowship: 12 months, a room, food, the labs, the machine shop and the compute at $0, a company in your name from day 1. 1 written application, no credentials needed. Apply at joinadastra.com

Sources: Science History Institute (prices converted to kilograms), International Aluminium Institute.
